section_summary: This section documents U.S. diplomatic and oil company responses to Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law and the proposed Manchukuo oil monopoly in late 1934. It includes correspondence, telegrams, conversation memoranda, an embassy despatch with enclosures, and duplicate or draft copies of several records. The central disputes concern compulsory oil stocks, import plans, refining rights, and the possible use of diplomatic or trade pressure.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmittal of petroleum conversation memoranda
subfiles.from: William Phillips, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sends confidential memoranda on Japan’s petroleum law and the proposed Manchukuo monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Lists enclosed conversations between State Department officers, oil company representatives, and other officials from August through November 1934.

subfiles.title: Teagle letter quoting Deterding cable
subfiles.about: Warns that acceptance of Japanese oil laws could set a precedent for government control elsewhere.
subfiles.summary: Quotes Sir Henri Deterding’s concern that similar demands worldwide would undermine commercial oil supply and emergency stocks.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Teagle’s letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Teagle’s letter and Deterding’s cable.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Teagle for forwarding Deterding’s warning about the wider effects of Japanese oil laws.

subfiles.title: Draft telegram on provisional import plans
subfiles.about: Reports company willingness to submit provisional plans if the Department agrees.
subfiles.summary: Draft conveys conditional agreement by Standard-Vacuum and Shell and indicates no departmental objection if companies and embassies approve.

subfiles.title: Coe cover letter forwarding comparison of French and Japanese petroleum laws
subfiles.about: Forwards a company letter comparing French and Japanese petroleum controls.
subfiles.summary: Coe sends the comparison and describes continuing consultations with London and Yokohama.

subfiles.title: Comparison of French and Japanese petroleum controls
subfiles.from: Kersey F. Coe, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Explains why Japanese petroleum controls are more burdensome than French rules.
subfiles.summary: Compares license terms, reserve requirements, compensation, and inspection powers. It also flags French provisions concerning government directed purchases and French participation in company management as possible models for future Japanese amendments.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reply to Coe
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the legal comparison and reports another U.S. protest over the Manchurian monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says the Department is considering the submitted materials and that the embassy made renewed representations on December 1.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Tokyo on oil company import plans
subfiles.about: States the Department’s conditional lack of objection to provisional import plans.
subfiles.summary: Shell and Standard-Vacuum favor the plan if both companies and the American and British embassies approve.

subfiles.title: Coe–Mackay telephone conversations
subfiles.about: Records calls arranging a meeting and discussing embassy knowledge and British representations.
subfiles.summary: Coe and Mackay discuss company officers traveling to Japan, uncertainty over what Ambassador Grew knows, and British action over Manchurian oil. Coe postpones his November 27 meeting pending information from London.

subfiles.title: Duplicate draft of Coe–Mackay conversation memorandum
subfiles.about: Repeats the November 26 telephone discussion in a noisier, incomplete copy.
subfiles.summary: Duplicates the discussion of the proposed meeting, embassy information, and British representations; the copy ends before the final paragraph.

subfiles.title: Draft copy of Grew despatch on American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports developments under Japan’s Petroleum Industry Law and proposes a treaty argument against compulsory reserves.
subfiles.summary: The despatch clarifies that Japanese participation in refining firms means at least half the capital. It describes rejected requests to delay import and storage plans, coordinated company and embassy responses, and limited concessions on qualifying stock. Grew suggests treating compelled reserves for wartime use as a possible military exaction under the 1911 treaty.

subfiles.title: Translated demand for supplemental oil plans, draft copy
subfiles.from: Japanese Department of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.to: J. C. Goold, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Demands a supplemental 1935 business plan by November 15.
subfiles.summary: Warns that failure to submit the plan could interfere with the company’s 1935 business.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum request for postponement, draft copy
subfiles.about: Requests more time to file the required supplemental plan.
subfiles.summary: Cites ongoing U.S.–Japanese discussions and the head office’s need to decide the company’s future.

subfiles.title: Dickover–Hasegawa conversation, draft copy
subfiles.about: Records Hasegawa’s view that Japan’s oil control scheme is commercially unworkable.
subfiles.summary: The damaged copy concerns the burden of compulsory storage on foreign oil companies.

subfiles.title: Neville–Kurusu conversation, draft copy
subfiles.about: Clarifies refining capital language and discusses a possible meeting with oil companies.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu explains that the Japanese phrase means at least half, offers written clarification, and proposes talks with Yoshino. Neville describes company fears about the November 15 deadline, quotas, and being pushed out of refined oil imports.

subfiles.title: Neville–Kurusu conversation, draft copy
subfiles.about: Discusses written guidance on stocks and difficulties with petroleum quotas.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu promises an English explanation of storage rules and acknowledges problems caused by rising demand and unequal prospects for foreign companies.

subfiles.title: Kurusu covering letter, draft copy
subfiles.about: Sends a Foreign Office explanation of compulsory oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: States that figures on application forms may later be altered for sufficient reasons.

subfiles.title: Explanation of legal obligation to hold oil, draft copy
subfiles.about: Explains quantities, timing, and permitted methods for holding compulsory oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: The guidance allows approved storage methods beyond prescribed tanks. It sets a reduced initial requirement for April–September 1935, followed by a gradual increase, and urges companies to apply for permission to use existing equipment.

subfiles.title: Hashimoto speech excerpt, draft copy
subfiles.about: Calls compulsory oil stocks a national defense burden.
subfiles.summary: Argues that the government should pay the costs of storage required for national defense.

subfiles.title: Handwritten file note
subfiles.about: Contains a largely illegible note concerning the Japanese oil issue.
subfiles.summary: The handwriting is too fragmentary to establish a clear substantive point.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs summary of despatch No. 1060
subfiles.about: Summarizes the embassy’s report on oil storage requirements and a possible treaty objection.
subfiles.summary: Notes British support for refusal to submit plans, possible easing of storage rules, and the argument that forced stocks constitute a military exaction.

subfiles.title: Grew despatch No. 1060 on American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s oil control measures, foreign company responses, and possible diplomatic arguments.
subfiles.summary: Grew clarifies that the disputed Japanese wording permits equal Japanese and foreign capital in a refinery. He reports demands for supplemental import and storage plans, coordinated foreign company responses, and Japanese explanations that modestly ease storage rules. He proposes examining whether forced wartime oil reserves breach the 1911 treaty prohibition on military exactions.

subfiles.title: Translated Japanese demand for supplemental plan
subfiles.from: Japanese Department of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.to: J. C. Goold, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Requires the company to file a supplemental 1935 plan by November 15.
subfiles.summary: Warns that a late response could disrupt approval of the 1935 business plan.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum request to postpone filing
subfiles.about: Asks to defer its supplemental filing during U.S.–Japanese discussions.
subfiles.summary: Says the New York head office needs the diplomatic talks to progress before deciding its future plans.

subfiles.title: Dickover conversation with Vice Admiral Hasegawa
subfiles.about: Records Hasegawa’s criticism of compulsory six month oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: Hasegawa agrees the storage scheme is commercially impossible and expects changes favoring foreign companies.

subfiles.title: Neville conversation with Kurusu on Petroleum Industry Law
subfiles.about: Clarifies capital requirements and discusses company objections to filing storage plans.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu says Japanese participation of at least half is sufficient for a refinery, promises written guidance, and seeks a meeting with company representatives. Neville explains company fears about quotas, the filing deadline, and loss of their import business.

subfiles.title: Neville conversation with Kurusu on quotas and stocks
subfiles.about: Discusses promised stockholding guidance and the impact of quotas on foreign firms.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu acknowledges difficulties caused by rising petroleum demand and doubts the present control system works well. Neville emphasizes that foreign companies face poorer prospects than Japanese refiners.

subfiles.title: Kurusu letter enclosing oil stockholding guidance
subfiles.about: Transmits an English explanation of compulsory oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: Says application figures may be changed later when the minister accepts the reasons.

subfiles.title: Explanations on Legal Obligation to Hold Oil
subfiles.about: Explains the staged oil reserve obligation and possible storage exceptions.
subfiles.summary: Oil importers must ultimately hold stocks equal to half the previous year’s imports, but may seek permission for smaller tanks or other methods. The initial 1935 amount is based on July–December 1934 imports, and the obligation rises gradually thereafter. Companies must apply for favorable treatment.

subfiles.title: Excerpt from K. Hashimoto speech
subfiles.about: Describes compulsory stockholding as a national defense measure.
subfiles.summary: Hashimoto says the requirement is costly and urges government reimbursement.

subfiles.title: Coe–Mackay conversation on Japan and Manchuria oil issues
subfiles.about: Records company proposals, diplomatic coordination, a possible refinery, and the Manchurian monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Coe reports Shell’s willingness to submit provisional import plans, a proposed meeting of oil company representatives in Shanghai, and a suggestion for a joint refinery. He discusses British diplomatic action, a crude oil tender for Manchuria, French oil controls, and information about the proposed monopoly’s sales arrangements.

subfiles.title: Shell London cable on provisional Form 4 return
subfiles.about: Proposes a provisional filing while preserving objections to Japanese oil controls.
subfiles.summary: Shell would file Form 4 conditionally, seeks clarification of future trade guarantees and refinery treatment, and favors coordinated diplomatic representations before detailed company talks.

subfiles.title: Shell London cable on company delegation and joint refinery
subfiles.about: Proposes a Shanghai meeting and asks about a joint refinery in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Godber, Walden, and Parker would confer before proceeding to Japan for commercial discussions.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable summary on Manchurian crude tender
subfiles.about: Reports a Nippon Oil tender for crude oil destined for Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The company plans to decline to quote, in line with Shell and Texas, unless circumstances change.

subfiles.title: May note on Shanghai correspondence
subfiles.about: Asks whether Shanghai letters should be passed to Hornbeck.
subfiles.summary: Notes promulgation of the monopoly law and that the Finance Department interviewers were Japanese.

subfiles.title: Shanghai report to New York on proposed Manchukuo oil monopoly
subfiles.from: F. J. Twogood, Standard-Vacuum Shanghai office
subfiles.about: Reports proposed monopoly arrangements and company responses in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The letter relays plans for government control of all oil sales, purchases from foreign companies on quotas, replacement of brands, and possible acquisition of distribution assets. It describes diplomatic contact, press coverage, and instructions to withhold requested data while awaiting a Japanese response.

subfiles.title: Moukden report on Hsinking Finance Department interview
subfiles.about: Reports an interview on the proposed Manchukuo government oil monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Names the Japanese officials present and begins outlining government control of oil agencies and sales; the report continues beyond this section.
